extracted.intended_audience: CEOs, CFOs, investor relations officers, general counsel and communications teams at public companies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and compliance standards for public-company disclosures — especially press releases, earnings calls, web/social media posts — covering non-GAAP financial measures, Regulation FD, and Regulation M-A filing/timing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory versus Voluntary Disclosure (triggers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many issuer disclosures are mandatory under the 1933 and 1934 Acts, SEC and stock exchange rules; virtually all other communications are voluntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandatory disclosures include: in any 1933 Act registration statement (e.g., IPO prospectus on Form S-1 and later Forms S-3); every 1934 Act annual or quarterly report (Form 10-K or 10-Q); events requiring a Form 8-K; when in the marketplace to buy or sell stock ("disclose or abstain"); to confirm or correct a rumor leaked from the company causing unusual trading likely to impact the marketplace; when required by stock exchange requirements; and to update prior statements that the market considers current or "evergreen." Voluntary communications include earnings calls, analyst conferences, website/social media posts, and discussions with analysts, investors or the press. Companies must apply SEC ground rules (Regulation G, Item 10(e) of Regulation S-K, Regulation FD, Regulation M-A) to voluntary and mandatory disclosures as applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory framework for voluntary disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Three key SEC regulations guide voluntary disclosure: Regulation G and Item 10(e) of Regulation S-K (non-GAAP measures), Regulation FD (selective disclosure), and Regulation M-A (M&A communications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand which rules apply to a given communication (e.g., whether it is filed or furnished affects Item 10(e) application). Use C&DIs (SEC compliance and disclosure interpretations) and interpretive releases to frame non-GAAP and FD compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Non-GAAP Financial Measures
rubrics_metrics.description: SEC defines non-GAAP financial measures as any numerical measure of historical or future performance, financial position or cash flow created by adjusting a comparable GAAP measure, generally by eliminating or including specific metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include adjusted EBITDA, adjusted free cash flow, net debt and KPIs calculated on a non-GAAP basis. Metrics based only on operating/statistical data (e.g., same-store sales, headcount) and ratios using only GAAP measures are not non-GAAP measures for these purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: KPIs and MD&A disclosure guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting KPIs or operating metrics (even if not non-GAAP), issuers should consider disclosure guidelines to avoid misleading investors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four recommended disclosures: (1) provide a clear definition and calculation method; (2) include a statement why the metric is useful and how management uses it; (3) consider whether estimates/assumptions underlying the metric need disclosure so the metric is not misleading; (4) consider whether differences in presentation from prior years need explanation or recasting of prior metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile non-GAAP measures to GAAP
rubrics_metrics.description: Any release of non-GAAP financial information must present the most directly comparable GAAP information and a reconciliation of the non-GAAP information to that GAAP information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies to all public releases containing non-GAAP measures — written, oral, telephonic, blogs, social media, websites, webcasts. For oral disclosures, companies can post the reconciliation on their website and provide the website address during the presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation S-K Item 10(e) additional filing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Item 10(e) applies to SEC-filed documents and imposes stricter requirements beyond Regulation G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Item 10(e) requires prominence of the comparable GAAP measure equal to or greater than the non-GAAP measure (e.g., earnings release headers should also contain the GAAP number) and an explanation of why management believes the non-GAAP measure is useful and, to the extent material, any additional purposes for its use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited or discouraged non-GAAP practices under Item 10(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Item 10(e) and SEC guidance prohibit or discourage certain presentations and adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibitions/discouragements include: using liquidity measures that exclude charges or liabilities requiring cash settlement other than EBIT or EBITDA; presenting non-GAAP performance measures adjusted to 'smooth' or eliminate items labeled nonrecurring/infrequent/unusual when those items are reasonably likely to recur within two years or where a similar charge/gain occurred in the previous two years; presenting non-GAAP measures on the face of financial statements, notes, or pro forma financial statements; and using titles/descriptions for non-GAAP measures that are confusingly similar to GAAP titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misleading non-GAAP adjustments and presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-GAAP measures should present a more accurate — not merely more favorable — view of the company; adjustments must not mislead investors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid: excluding normal recurring cash operating expenses necessary to run the business; inconsistent presentation across periods; selectively excluding nonrecurring charges while not excluding nonrecurring gains; substituting company-specific revenue recognition or measurement methods for GAAP. Be particularly cautious about 'individually tailored' metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trap guidance: rules apply to all public communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation G rules apply to all public communications whether filed or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SEC expects consistent presentation of non-GAAP information across press releases, analyst calls, slide shows, webcasts. Do not disclose non-GAAP metrics in less formal channels unless prepared to include them in 10-K/10-Q filings as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation FD selective disclosure rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation FD requires issuers to publicly disclose material nonpublic information if a company or person acting on its behalf voluntarily discloses it to securities market professionals or to security holders when it is reasonably foreseeable they would trade on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If disclosure to a limited audience is intentional, public disclosure must be made simultaneously; in practice, companies usually publicly distribute material information prior to selective disclosure. If disclosure is unintentional, public disclosure must be made promptly (see timing rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for curing unintentional Regulation FD disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: If disclosure was unintentional, the company must make public disclosure promptly after the inadvertent disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promptly means by the later of: 24 hours after the unintentional disclosure; or, if the next trading day begins more than 24 hours later, prior to the beginning of the next trading day. The SEC's 24‑hour clock begins when a senior official learns of the disclosure and recognizes the information as material and nonpublic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curing unintentional disclosures (practical steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an inadvertent selective disclosure occurs, companies should promptly disseminate the material nonpublic information broadly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include issuing a press release or appropriate website/social media disclosure, and furnishing the curative press release on Form 8-K (Item 7.01) to ensure broad dissemination. Item 7.01 can serve as a 'super-press release.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference/presentation scripting to avoid inadvertent disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid inadvertent disclosures during unscripted Q&A at conferences, presenters should 'follow the script' and prepare in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior to presenting, disclose in a press release or Form 8-K the material information you want to be able to discuss. Arrange a pre-announced webcast. Have your IRO or CFO monitor and help the CEO decline to answer unscripted questions that may require disclosure of material nonpublic information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality definition and factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Material information is that which a reasonable investor would consider important in making an investment decision or that would significantly alter the total mix of information available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No bright-line test; materiality depends on probability and magnitude of contingent events and qualitative factors. Use SEC and Supreme Court standards and consider SAB 99 guidance when assessing materiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hot buttons of materiality (seven categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: The SEC lists seven categories issuers should review carefully when determining materiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories: earnings information (historical or future estimates); mergers/acquisitions/tender offers/joint ventures; new products/discoveries/developments with customers or suppliers; changes of control or senior management; change in auditors; events regarding securities (defaults, splits, dividends, sales); bankruptcy or receivership. Earnings estimates are particularly sensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: SAB 99 and small-amount materiality guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: SAB 99 rejects using fixed dollar or percentage thresholds alone to judge non-materiality and warns that qualitative factors can render even small misstatements material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule-of-thumb measures (e.g., 5%) may be used only as a starting point. Examples of qualitative indicators: masking changes in earnings/forward trends; hiding failure to meet analyst consensus; changing loss to income; affecting regulatory compliance or debt covenants; concealing unlawful transactions; affecting compensation thresholds. SEC may assess materiality in hindsight (stock price/volume reaction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Earnings call compliance procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended pre-call, call, and post-call practices to comply with Regulation FD and non-GAAP disclosure rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before the call: issue a press release/web notice several days/weeks in advance (include access info and state call may cover material developments); announce earnings by press release and furnish to SEC under Item 2.02 of Form 8-K; post all financial/statistical data and any required reconciliations on the company's website before the call. During/after call: hold call within 48 hours after the Form 8-K filing; if call includes new material nonpublic information and occurs >48 hours after the Form 8-K, file a new Form 8-K furnishing a transcript within four business days after the call; post audio/transcript of newly disclosed material promptly and keep website postings accessible (SEC encourages at least one year) and archive with disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Website and social media as recognized channels for Regulation FD
rubrics_metrics.description: Posting material information on a company's website or social media can satisfy Regulation FD public disclosure if the outlet is a recognized distribution channel and meets dissemination/time criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three tests: (1) Recognized Channel — has the company taken steps to alert the market it will use the website/social account to distribute info?; (2) Broad Dissemination — is the posting accessible to the securities marketplace generally and designed to lead investors to disclosures?; (3) Time to Absorb — did posting give investors enough time to absorb/react, considering company size, steps to alert investors, nature/complexity of info, and dissemination efforts? Include cautionary legend in Form 10-K/10-Q describing intent to use website/social channels and which accounts will be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media and personal account risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees' or officers' personal social media posts may violate Regulation FD if the company hasn't prepared those outlets as recognized channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train employees/officers/directors that personal posts may be perceived as company statements. Create social media policy, designate recognized channels, and provide review/approval processes. Example: DraftKings CEO's personal posts led to SEC scrutiny because accounts were not identified as distribution channels and a timely company disclosure did not follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions from Regulation FD
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain communications are exempt from Regulation FD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemptions include discussions with persons who expressly agree to maintain confidentiality (NDA, written or verbal); ordinary-course business disclosures to customers/suppliers; disclosures by foreign private issuers (subject to qualifications); disclosure to persons who owe a duty of trust/confidence (lawyers, bankers, financial advisors, accountants); and most road show communications in connection with 1933 Act registered offerings (with exceptions: Form S-8 and Form S-3 resale registrations are subject to FD).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosures to rating agencies and NRSROs
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures to nationally recognized statistical rating organizations (NRSROs) are not subject to Regulation FD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although NRSROs are not 'covered persons' for FD purposes, a cautious issuer may ask smaller non-NRSROs to sign NDAs before sharing confidential information during rating reviews because NRSROs have regulatory obligations limiting use of the information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability limitations under Regulation FD
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation FD limits issuer liability to knowing and reckless conduct and does not create private rights of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation FD is not an antifraud rule; however, other antifraud liabilities (e.g., Rule 10b-5) remain applicable and the SEC actively enforces selective disclosure matters. Materiality will often be assessed in hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward-looking statements safe harbor requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify for the statutory safe harbor for forward-looking statements, statements must be accompanied by meaningful cautionary language and (for written statements) important factors that could cause actual results to differ materially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boilerplate disclaimers are insufficient. Practical tips: tailor cautionary language to specific forward-looking statements, disclose assumptions underlying each forward-looking statement, identify a variety of reasons for deviation, describe magnitude of specific risks, and update risk factors/cautionary statements in SEC filings to remain current.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral forward-looking statements guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral forward-looking statements must include meaningful cautionary language referencing readily available written documents containing more detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaningful oral caution should declare that additional information on factors that could cause actual results to differ materially is contained in a recent Form 10-K or 10-Q (or other readily available written document). Avoid relying on boilerplate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation M-A filing requirements for M&A communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies must file with the SEC any written communication made in connection with or relating to a business combination that is provided to the public or persons not party to the transaction, starting from the first public announcement until the transaction closes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing must occur on or before the date of first use. Each Regulation M-A written communication must include a prominently displayed legend advising investors to read the relevant registration/proxy/tender offer statement and directing them to the SEC's website for copies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation M-A exceptions (no filing required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain communications do not need to be filed under Regulation M-A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No filing required for: factual business information that relates solely to ordinary business matters; internal communications provided solely to parties to the transaction; and oral communications (but posting audio/video/slides on a website requires filing a transcript).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay among Regulations M-A, G, S-K, and FD for forecasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules overlap for forecasts used in M&A contexts and for forecasts included in other documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forecasts used by financial advisors to render an opinion materially related to the business combination and disclosed to comply with Regulation M-A are excluded from Regulation G and Item 10(e) (no GAAP reconciliation required). However, if the same non-GAAP measures/forecasts are disclosed in a registration statement or proxy statement, Regulation G and Item 10(e) will apply and reconciliation rules may be triggered. When both M-A and FD apply, file in a format that satisfies M-A but comply with FD timing (prior or simultaneous public disclosure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate disclosure policy recommended elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'best in class' disclosure policy should include specific elements to ensure compliance with non-GAAP, FD, and M-A rules and to take advantage of safe harbors for forward-looking statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy elements include: (1) Non-GAAP measures — ensure presentation is not misleading and reconcile to most directly comparable GAAP measure; (2) Spokespersons — designate procedures for drafting, reviewing, approving, and distributing material communications and specify who may speak for the company (chair, CEO, CFO, IRO, etc.); (3) Materiality — have a process, with counsel as necessary, to determine materiality and need for disclosure; (4) Cautionary language — include legends for forward-looking statements; (5) Earnings calls — adhere to recommended procedures (pre-release, posting reconciliations, timing, transcripts); (6) One-on-one calls/meetings — limit timing to post‑earnings-call until blackout periods, prepare scripts and limit responses to elaboration of previously disclosed or generally known information; (7) Analyst projections and previous earnings guidance — do not confirm previous guidance or individual analyst projections; (8) Extraordinary transactions/unusual market activity — generally do not respond to questions unless legally required; (9) Treat media interviews as subject to Regulation FD; (10) M&A communications — file written communications with appropriate legend before public disclosure.
